For immediate support, you can jump to the resources by clicking on the topics here:Immediate Crisis, Sexual Abuse, Childhood Abuse, Domestic Violence, Mental Health, Depression and SuicideI am really glad you’ve found your way here. Whether that’s because you’ve read one of my books and found it difficult to leave the pages even after the last word or because you’ve stumbled across a blog full of sensitive material or you happened to be at an event where you heard me speak and curiosity tugged you closer, I am glad you’re here.  You’ve likely seen it written on other pages by now, or heard me say it, but your story matters.   We all have one. I am many things.  First, I am a mother.  My heart beats because of them and my world revolves around them. Their names are Breathe and Alight: breathe because breath means life and to breathe means to actively sustain life; the verb form of alight means to descend, to light; the adjective form means to illuminate or set on fire. Alight was an answer to a direct prayer; she alighted onto my life as a gift from God but it was the adjective form that bought her the name. She illuminates my life. Together, they mean illuminated life then.  They are exactly that for me. I’m also a writer, an advocate, a revenue management leader. And I am a survivor of rape. From the age of five, I’ve understood on an intimate level what it means to be held down and forced to do things you don’t want to do. The lessons survivors learn – don’t trust people, the system won’t help you, your body isn’t safe – I learned too. And I’ve spent half my life digging through the rubble, keeping the diamonds and turning ashes into dandelions through storytelling. I spend my nights researching the absolute worst in humanity just so I can find reasons to keep stumbling in the dark, hands outstretched, feeling my way through the world until I see it: light. It was my first speaking engagement in front of a crowd of people. I stood in a classroom at a college in Memphis that was full of students and it was being recorded and I knew there were many more watching. I had spent countless hours writing, rewriting, timing and agonizing over every word in this speech. I worried they might mock me. I worried they might not believe me. I worried they might blame me. I feared that I might receive a reaction that would confirm every awful thing I had been taught to believe. Then I got to the word. That moment in the speech – it was early, quick after the introduction – where I was supposed to say it. Say what happened. I was only a few years past initial disclosure and most of my talking had been through the written word. The word rape terrified me. Worse, it made liquid shame run through my whole body. Instead, I was more comfortable saying, I was hurt. Hurt was my euphemism; it was my protection. But as I stood looking at the crowd of college students staring back at me, something made me stop. If I said hurt, someone in that audience was going to be confused. Hurt how? Molested? Beaten? Verbally abused?  Betrayed?  There were as many ways to misunderstand that word as there were students in the room. Even worse, I’d had the training. I knew the statistics. In that room, there were dozens of survivors and each of them were likely in different stages: some of them could be in an actively abusive situation, some might have just disclosed to someone, someone might be pressing Congress for a new bill. My whole purpose in giving the speech was not to sell a single book. It was not to grow readership. It was to tell a survivor that someone else got it. I wanted a survivor to recognize her or himself in me. The only way that could happen is I said the word.  So I did. Out loud. In front of a hundred or more people. My body immediately responded: my face heated with shame, my head dropped to avoid seeing reactions, I stumbled over the rest of the sentence, the world blurred behind unshed tears. Anyone watching immediately knew I wasn’t a healed anything; I was ashamed and saying it anyway. No one was unkind.In fact, someone approached me afterward and told me she heard me. I went home and brutally attacked that word rape by researching the full history. I didn’t just google it, I spent hours researching its history. And one definition stopped me in my tracks. Rape originally meant to seize, to take by force. The word that got me was “seize.” Because something was missing, something was taken. I felt it in my bones. I missed and ached for the little girl, the innocence that I barely remembered. What happened did seize something. When I applied that definition instead of thinking about it as a physical act, I could say it.The word “hero” comes from ancient Greek where it meant protector and has evolved to mean someone with exceptional courage. The word brave originally implied a sense of wildness. So, the phrase brave hero means someone who wildly protects someone or something. Protect didn’t originally mean save. It simply meant to shield.  A shield can be anything that keeps something harmful at a safer distance. One of the most powerful shields against the lies of abuse, against the fear, against nightmares, against hopelessness, against all the tender things trauma attacks us with is conversation. When we invite someone to hold space for us so that we can share how we are feeling and what we are thinking, we shield our minds and hearts from more pain. We don’t have to say anything we don’t want to say. We don’t have to share details we don’t want to. Sometimes the shield is simply sitting beside someone without having to pretend we’re okay.  It is the wildest, bravest act of protecting the part of you who needs someone. The hero in this room is you.  Below is a list of resources — phone numbers, websites and places to begin — that are safe. They are lanterns flickering for you. If you’d like to know a bit more about what it might be like to reach out, I am a trained hotline specialist. You can read about what you might expect here. Whenever you are ready, these places are here for you. You do not have to know exactly what kind of help you need before reaching for it. Some of these organizations provide immediate, confidential support; others offer education, peer connection, longer-term resources, or help finding services near you. You are allowed to begin with the one that feels most possible.And — if what you need is help in sharing, this disclosure guide is yours. Free to download, print, and make yours. Saccharine (2026)A medical student who is self-conscious about her body starts taking an unknown pill – a strange sort of capsule – to lose weight. This decision triggers an unexpected and terrifying side effect, unleashing a supernatural force that increasingly takes over her daily life.Yet another Australian film I didn’t like. Seriously!!! I think that within the first three-quarters of an hour, I already knew I was going to give this film a very low rating. My disappointment is all the greater given that the theme of eating disorders, within the context of a horror film, seemed quite innovative in the 2020s. The film does feature a few very beautiful shots, particularly of bodily fluids and the interior of bodies. Yes, unfortunately it’s reminiscent of The Substance (2024), which I hated. The film’s main flaw is that it’s a mix of Coralie Fargeat’s film and Grave (2016), which I didn’t like at all either. That’s saying something! Two female directors I can’t stand. As for Grave, it’s the carnal aspect centred on food that puts me off.The film might have been more successful if it had been cut by a good half an hour. As it stands, it’s rather repetitive and very boring. The storyline centred on the heroine’s family, which is very interesting, would have deserved more screen time. Two parents doing their best, but their best isn’t very high. Between the father, who struggles to do anything, and the mother, who goes overboard. In fact, she reminded me of my own worries. Those mothers who are always wanting to tidy and clean their children’s bedrooms without realising that they’re intruding on a private world they can’t possibly understand. We throw things away and clean up without realising that this mess might have had its own significance, symbolic or otherwise.We know that stories about weight will attract an audience, just as we know it’s just as easy to have a hit with a film about money. Like when people come into a fortune and decide to keep it to themselves without telling anyone else. So it’s the same with stories where someone finds a miracle solution for losing weight. These are indeed constant, permanent and eternal problems for people in our society. What a sad world!This film is, of course, rather despicable. The subject matter is repulsive, especially when you discover what’s in the so-called miracle pills. The atmosphere is as grim as you could wish for. The lead actress is truly unsettling, which does, however, demonstrate a certain talent.But there comes a point where it all gets completely ridiculous, and from that moment on, I gradually lost interest. It hadn’t really managed to hold my attention right from the start.At least this film doesn’t really make you fancy a bite to eat. That’s the cool thing about it if you’re watching it with the aim of losing a few kilos! Saccharine offers nothing particularly meaty or substantial to sink your teeth into.Forrest Gump says “Life is like a box of chocolates”, but not quite so for obese people. It’s glaringly obvious that this film lacks subtlety.We can add a third film that I hated to the list of what this film reminded me of. Indeed, Antiviral (2012) by Cronenberg Jr, Brandon, can round off my list of a quartet of despicable films to avoid. Except for the most twisted among us, of course. Fans of the macabre, gore and grim, sickening atmospheres can rush headlong into these films without hesitation.If the plot invokes the miracle weight-loss pill, the filmmaker would do well to find the formula for a successful pace, surprise and dramatic tension – essential ingredients for concocting genuine intellectual satisfaction. Natalie Erika James, an American, Australian and Japanese director, screenwriter and producer, is no doubt trying to show that she can shock and disgust even more than men, whilst thinking she’s doing a better job. But with slow service and bland food, it’s a definite NO!The trio of leading actresses do a fine job. Midori Francis, Madeleine Madden, and Danielle Macdonald are quite good, but Danielle Macdonald is excellent. I would have loved to see more of her in this film. All her scenes are the best in my opinion.Somewhere between body horror and a ghost film, Saccharine, Natalie Erika James’s third feature film, suffers from a thematic overload, tackling themes such as the cult of thinness, eating disorders and female desire. The sweetness is there, as are the intentions, but it doesn’t quite hit the spot. ⭐Rating: 1 out of 5.

Success?
The word for the day at Ragtag Daily Prompt is successI don’t “hate” a lot of things in life. I did when I was younger until I eventually reached a point where I realized it took a lot of energy to hate. But “success” is a word I hate.I used to have a friend (RIP 11 years now☹️) who would judge everyone and everything. We would sit and be miserable together and he’d say stuff like, “He’s had a lot of girlfriends, he’s really a success”, or “He’s really successful, he has a good job and a lot of money.” You get the idea. And of course the underlying idea behind everything is that he and I, by virtue of our not having the things that he defined as “success” in life, like girlfriends, or glamorous careers, or fancy cars, or big houses, or lots of children, were failures.Worse, for me, was that his standards of success and failure, they all flew in the face of my hard-earned (and expensive) belief that we don’t judge our insides with other people’s outsides. And as it turned out, hard-earned doesn’t always mean easily kept so there I was crying in my pizza along with him, failure that I was.Ok, I don’t totally hate the word success because it has some legitimate uses, but I hate using the word “success” to define a person’s place in life, or in contrast, to indirectly label, or imply, someone a failure. And I’m pretty much back to not judging my insides with other people’s outsides.Kiss a little baby, give the world a smileAnd if you take an inch, give ’em back a mile‘Cause if you lie like a rug and you don’t give a damnYou’re never gonna be as happy as a clam

A new ‘Carrie’ coming — because bullying is still relevant
Photo by La Fabbrica Dei Sogni on UnsplashIt was over 10 years ago that the 2013 “Carrie” remake was the talk of the town.Before I saw it, I blogged about it, along with the other “Carrie” movies:  October we have “Carrie” returning in an Amazon Prime mini-series. I can’t wait! The novel by “Carrie” by Stephen King, back in 1974, was absolutely brilliant. It’s the story of about a shy, awkward high school student abused by both her Christian fundamentalist mother and school bullies. Then along came all the movies — and even a musical which I didn’t see but I keep meaning to see if I could find something on YouTube. When the developer Mike Flannagan was asked why yet another “Carrie,” he spoke about how bullying is still relevant today.Yes, over 50 years later, we have not evolved. Kids still bully each other.In the foreword to my book, “I Don’t Want to Be Like You” — which you can order directly through my publisher (Higher Ground) —  I speak about how I feel bullying is even worse today than when I was bullied in the 1970s. ( share that bullying is worse nowadays because on the online and social media experience. In the 1970s we had refuge, being able to temporarily shut it off. Being safe in our homes, in our rooms, listening to records, we can dream of a better life once we graduated. We would never see the bullies again.A side note, a little plug for my antibullying YouTube channel because over the weekend someone said that they liked it. I haven’t updated in ages, but here it is:  now, back to Carrie….Carrie’s telekinetic powers of destroying the entire school can be a metaphor for that. I like to believe that Carrie’s death is also a metaphor that the old Carrie who was bullied is no longer alive. She’s now the beautiful confident Carrie. It was all a bad dream. Yes, she was the prom queen and she lived happily ever after with Tommy Ross. That could be the positive ending that those being bullied need to see, because shy awkward people can have their happy ending. But even though Carrie’s ending wasn’t a good one, it still sent a strong message that you reep what you sow. Bullies may not die, but their anger will definitely eat them alive, which is just the same as being dead. The ending was a lose/lose for everyone but the bullies definitely did not win. It’s not exactly a movie of justice, but it’s still a lesson.
